newsitem.title: SUDAN: Southern Sudanese in no hurry to sign full peace.
newsitem.headline: Southern Sudanese in no hurry to sign full peace.

text.p: Southern Sudanese factions have agreed to wait before turning their peace charter with the Khartoum government into a full peace agreement, a government newspaper said on Friday.
The factions wanted to give active rebel groups and leaders in southern Sudan a chance to open a dialogue with the government, the newspaper al-Ingaz al-Watani reported.

"The delay is due to reasons concerning administrative arrangements and foreign contacts being undertaken by southern factions and leaders who have signed the charter," it added, quoting Mohamad al-Amin Khalifa, the secretary general of the government's Higher Council for Peace.
The peace charter was first signed in April with two small former rebel factions and others have since come out in support of the government's peace initiative.
But the mainstream Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), the group which does most of the fighting, has dismissed the charter as a sham and continues to fight government troops.
The rebels are fighting for greater autonomy for the black African south against the Arab and Islamised north of the country, which dominates the national government.

The charter says the unity of Sudan should be preserved within its recognised borders. It also offers the southerners a referendum "to determine their political aspirations," but only after peace and stability and a reasonable level of development have been established in the south.

The SPLA, led by former Sudanese army colonel John Garang, says it does not trust the present government, which is dominated by Islamists intent on extending Islamic law and which describes the war in the south as a jihad (holy war).
It is not immediately clear what form the proposed final peace agreement would take without the SPLA taking part.

Sudanese media have reported another defection from the ranks of the SPLA, this time by Daniel Kot Mathews, a former governor of Upper Nile state. Mathews, a Nuer by ethnicity, announced in London he supported the peace charter, they said.

The official news agency SUNA said on Friday that 43 fellow former Nuer rebels crossed the Ethiopian border into the eastern state of Gedaref on Thursday after handing themselves in at the Sudanese embassy in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.
